input: The performance of a mechanical-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over the course of one summer month, and the data collected provide a useful indication of how the tower behaves under warm-weather conditions. Over the logging period, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, which is broadly representative of the summer conditions at the site. The tower operated with an approach of 5 K and a range of 5 K during this period. The approach, which describes how closely the cooled water temperature approaches the wet-bulb temperature, and the range, which describes the drop in water temperature as the water passes through the tower, are the two figures that are conventionally used to characterise the performance of a cooling tower of this kind. Taken together, the figures suggest that the tower was performing in line with what might be expected for a unit of this type under the conditions experienced, and they provide a baseline against which future performance could be compared. It is important to bear in mind, however, that the performance was characterised over a single summer month only. Performance outside the logged month, and in particular at the much lower wet-bulb temperatures that occur in winter, was not measured, so it would be inappropriate to extrapolate these results to the winter period or to treat them as a complete characterisation of the tower's behaviour across the full range of conditions that it will experience throughout the year of operation at the site.
target: A mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 27 °C. The tower ran at an approach of 5 K and a range of 5 K. The approach is the difference between the cooled-water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature: it states how close the tower brings the water to the limit the air imposes. The range is the fall in water temperature across the tower: it states the cooling the water receives in one pass. Both figures are stated for the flows and the loading of the logged month, and they move if the plant moves the water flow or the heat load away from that month's values. Read together, the two figures characterise the tower for the logged month: the cooling it delivered and the margin it held against the air condition, on the water and air flows that the plant ran during that month. They are summer figures. Performance outside the logged month was not measured, and at winter wet-bulb temperatures in particular the tower's behaviour is unrecorded. A tower that holds its approach in summer may hold it more easily in winter, when the air is cooler and the same water flow meets a larger driving force, or it may be limited instead by water distribution or fan operation under different loads; the logged month cannot distinguish these cases, because the conditions that separate them did not occur while the instruments were running. The figures stand as a summer characterisation of the tower. A winter figure would need a winter logging period of the same kind, and the two together would still leave the shoulder seasons unmeasured.
